contract.goal: reach a recipient inside the product: IN_APP as a passive destination settled in the fan-out transaction, plus a recipient-owned inbox they read back
contract.output: notification-service only - ChannelClass on ChannelType, IN_APP settled in-transaction with no NotificationChannel bean, notification_inbox_item + _content tables, recipient-facing inbox read API, read-anchored retention, per-category-class suppression fallback, and the 8 mechanical checks from specs/enforcement-triad
constraints: no new in-repo dependency and no POM change - notification-service already compiles against every module needed
no NotificationChannel bean for IN_APP: a transport is contractually forbidden from touching the database
no IN_APP body in notification_delivery_content: that table is purged at content-ttl 7d
no read-state field on any delivery entity: it is a hot claim-query row, not a user-owned document
no preference rule may read the ChannelType.IN_APP constant - it consults ChannelClass
every transport classification is a mandatory enum constructor argument, so the compiler is the check
QueryDSL against generated Q-types only - this change claims no native-SQL carve-out and adds no fenced package
no OperationResponse on an inbox endpoint, no cache, no second ProblemDetail pipeline, no second redaction mask
the four new ArchUnit rules live in notification-service's own test sources, never in architecture-rules
no vacuous rule for the push transport this change deliberately does not add

decisions: IN_APP is a settlement in the fan-out transaction, not a NotificationChannel - the work queue exists to keep a third-party network off a pooled connection, and this destination is the same Postgres the transaction is already writing to (design.md D1)
a separate ui-notification-service was considered and rejected for now; D1 is the seam to cut along if read volume justifies it, because everything on the inbox side is already a separate aggregate

ChannelClass is a mandatory enum constructor argument rather than a Set or a lookup table, so a new transport without a classification does not compile - the compiler is a stronger check than any triad rule (design.md D2)
the inbox is two tables mirroring the delivery/content split, for the same two reasons, but with a different retention window - which is exactly why it cannot be the same table (design.md D3)
the fallback is keyed by category class in configuration, never a request field, for the same reason PreferenceEvaluator gives for the transactional bypass (design.md D4)
gate.sh takes the bare artifactId and rejects the ':' form it prints for mvn; the real gate also runs check_image_pins.sh and check_api_baseline.sh, which the first draft of tasks.md omitted

1.3 evidence, verified not assumed: adding IN_APP to ChannelKind alone fails the build with 'The following constants from the source enum have no corresponding constant in the target enum and must be be mapped via adding additional mappings: IN_APP' at NotificationDtoMapper.java:161. The MapStruct triad check is real.

the mandatory-classification design (D2) paid off immediately and unplanned: adding IN_APP broke three pre-existing exhaustive switches, each of which was a decision the new transport genuinely needed - NotificationConfigurationValidator.slowestChannelTimeout (no provider call -> ZERO), ChannelRuntime.settings (no dispatch settings -> throw, because every caller is dispatch-path-only), DefaultRecipientResolver.addressOf (no address by construction -> null). The compiler walked the change through all three.

kept those switches exhaustive instead of adding a `default` arm or an isPassive() `continue`: exhaustiveness is the check that surfaced all three, and a default arm would silently answer for the next transport that does have a timeout. Each IN_APP arm is spelled out with its reason.

ChannelRuntime.settings throws for a passive channel rather than returning zeroed settings: a zeroed ChannelSettings would rate-limit the inbox to nothing and silently stop delivering it, whereas a throw is a loud bug at the point the settlement leaked into the queue.

DefaultRecipientResolver needed two passive guards, not one, and both are latent bugs if omitted: a null address short-circuits to Optional.empty() (a terminal delivery), so without the guard every single in-app delivery would have gone terminal; and resolveAddress would otherwise have produced a ResolvedRecipient with a null userId, i.e. an inbox item with no owner. Both ask isPassive() rather than naming IN_APP.

tasks.md named the wrong classes for phase 2's verification and for the settlement site; corrected in place. The settlement is in DeliveryFanOutService.settle, not NotificationServiceImpl. There was no PreferenceEvaluatorTest, SuppressionServiceTest or digest test to extend, so 2.1/2.2 are proved by a new PreferenceEvaluatorTest and 2.3/2.4 by a new PassiveChannelSettlementTest (Mockito over DeliveryFanOutService), each scenario paired with an interrupting-channel control.

THIRD passive guard found, and the most dangerous: DeliveryFanOutService skipped any channel whose ChannelRegistry lookup was empty, on the grounds that a row nobody can send is a dead letter blaming the recipient for a deployment gap. Having no bean is exactly how IN_APP is built, so that guard would have silently dropped every in-app notification while still answering 202. Exempted by isPassive(), with an interrupting-channel control asserting the guard still fires.

2.5 evidence, verified not assumed: replacing channel.isPassive() with channel == ChannelType.IN_APP in PreferenceEvaluator fails InAppCarveOutRulesTest with 'Rule ... should access field ChannelType.IN_APP ... was violated (1 times)'. Reverted. The ArchUnit rule is real.

TENSION with an existing stated decision, resolved rather than ignored: DeliveryFanOutService's javadoc says rendering is deliberately NOT done at fan-out (it would double ingress latency, and a template about to be corrected would bake old wording into queued rows). An in-app delivery has no later send step, so for it that reasoning does not apply - and deferring the render to read time is not merely awkward but impossible, because retention.recipient-data-ttl scrubs the variable map at 7d while an unread item may live for months. So IN_APP renders in the fan-out transaction (design.md D5) and the javadoc must say why the two answers differ.

scripts/check_migrations.sh reads git ls-files, so a new changeset reads as 'which no module ships' until it is at least intent-to-added (git add -N). Not a defect in the change; worth knowing before a third attempt is wasted on the SQL.

REAL DEFECT found by the integration suite and fixed, not worked around: opt-out setting keys are derived from ChannelType.name().toLowerCase(), and a setting key is ^[a-z][a-z0-9]*([.-][a-z0-9]+)*$ with NO underscore. IN_APP is the first multi-word constant, so user.notifications.opt-out.all.in_app was rejected when the SettingDefinitionRegistry bean was built - failing the whole application at startup, several beans deep, and taking 13 integration tests with it. Fixed at the single source both the declaration and the lookup go through (NotificationSettings.keySegment, _ -> -), giving .in-app.

chose to transform the key rather than rename the constant to INAPP: the enum name is published on the wire, in a column and in log lines, and it should not be made worse everywhere to suit one key format. Encoded twice per the repo rule - ChannelSettingKeyTest now asserts every constant maps to a key the settings module accepts, and pins .in-app so a transform producing 'inapp' (also pattern-valid) cannot pass silently.

3.5 scope stated honestly: InboxSchemaIT asserts the two FK delete actions (SET NULL for the delivery, CASCADE for content), the owner index, the partial retention index predicate and the nullability, because none of those is visible to Hibernate's own mapping validation. It does NOT execute the --rollback statements; both are DROP TABLE of a table the same changeset created and check_migrations.sh fails if either is absent.

4.5 and 4.6 are test METHODS in InAppSettlementIT (noTransportSupportsInApp, claimIgnoresInAppDeliveries) rather than the separate NoInAppChannelBeanIT / ClaimIgnoresInAppIT classes tasks.md named: both need the same Spring context and the same fixtures, and a second @SpringBootTest class for one assertion each would double the context count for no isolation gain. The production javadoc that named the two classes was repointed at the real methods - a dangling reference to a test class that does not exist is exactly the prose-that-rots this repo's rules exist to prevent.

4.7 evidence, verified not assumed: injecting all three violations at once (a readAt field on NotificationDeliveryEntity, @Filterable on InboxItemEntity.ownerUserId, a DeliveryContentRepository field in InAppSettlement) failed exactly the three new ArchUnit rules - 'Tests run: 4, Failures: 3'. All reverted. The read-state rule reports 2 violations because the generated Q-type mirrors the field, which is harmless and arguably better coverage.

InAppSettlement renders all three template parts (subject, body.html, body.txt) and the in-app template directory segment is in_app, matching the enum name, while the settings opt-out key segment is in-app. The asymmetry is deliberate and commented in the template: a setting key is constrained by a pattern that admits no underscore and a directory name is not constrained at all.

DELIVERED and not SENT for a settled in-app delivery: SENT means 'handed to a provider that has not confirmed', and with no provider the intermediate state would be unobservable and no receipt would ever resolve it. Metric is recordSendSucceeded rather than recordDeliveryEnqueued, because counting it as enqueued would make the queue gauges claim work that does not exist - which is the number an operator uses to decide whether the queue is moving.
user instructed 2026-10-09 to ignore check_api_baseline.sh and continue; its failure stays recorded in failures and is NOT a pass. The remaining done_when commands still have to pass on their own.

5.4's ArchUnit rule (owner not @Filterable) was already written in 4.7 alongside the other three, since all four belong in one InAppCarveOutRulesTest and were proved together; 5.4 is ticked on that evidence rather than re-done.

dropped the injected Clock from InboxService in favour of Instant.now(), matching every other timestamp in this service: an unqualified Clock bean is a by-type injection hazard the day a starter with its own Clock lands on the classpath, and no assertion in these tests needs a fixed clock - they are about ordering, nullness, and a value being unchanged across a repeat.

MarkAllReadIT drives the bulk update through a TransactionTemplate rather than annotating the class @Transactional: a transactional test would run the update and all assertions in one rolled-back transaction, so a statement that only appeared to work before commit would still pass.

a JPA bulk update needs an ambient transaction - calling items.markAllRead outside one fails with InvalidDataAccessApiUsage. Production is covered because InboxService.markAllRead is @Transactional; it is only the direct-repository test that had to supply one.

the inbox list excludes dismissed items but findOwned includes them: dismissing is not deleting, and a client holding a link to an item it just dismissed must still be able to open it. Both halves are asserted in MarkAllReadIT.

the filterable-surface document is served by odata-filter's own FilterMetadataController, not by a second endpoint in this service: publication is opt-in per entity via @FilterPolicy(metadataName=...), so the inbox sets metadataName and application.yml sets odata.filter.metadata.base-path. The delivery's surface stays unpublished on purpose - its audience is support, not a browser.

the inbox endpoints gate on isAuthenticated() with no role, and TestPrincipals gained a role-free recipient(subject) for exactly that reason: reading one's own notifications is not a privilege anybody grants, and an IT running as admin would pass against endpoints accidentally gated on a role.

6.3's byte-identical assertion needed three fields normalised, and each for a stated reason rather than to make it pass: instance echoes the URI the caller themselves sent, timestamp is the clock, and traceId's presence depends on whether a trace context was active rather than on whether the item exists. type, title, status, code and the wording of detail are all still compared, which is what the oracle concern is actually about.

notification-service had NO message-bundle parity test before this change - a pre-existing gap, since bundle key-set parity is a platform rule. Added MessageBundleParityTest following file-action's precedent (key sets, .title companions, no blank value, matching placeholders, UTF-8 read explicitly because Properties.load(InputStream) is ISO-8859-1 by contract and would have made every Cyrillic message mojibake). It found no pre-existing violations.

InboxItemView/InboxItemResponse deliberately carry no owner field: the caller IS the owner, so the field could only repeat what the client already knows, and a field on a response is the one a client sends back - which is the parameter this API must never accept. Asserted in InboxScopingIT.

added a SECOND startup relation check beyond the one tasks.md asked for: inbox-ttl must not be SHORTER than content-ttl. The asked-for check (inbox-content-ttl <= inbox-ttl) catches an orphaned body; this one catches the likelier mistake, because the inbox windows are months where content-ttl is days and the first instinct on reading that is that one is a typo - 'correcting' the inbox down to 7d would make the inbox expire before the push attempt it exists to outlive.

the unread-ceiling purge is logged at WARN on its own line and excluded from the routine purge total, rather than folded in: every other number is housekeeping, while this one is 'we destroyed notifications their recipients were meant to read and never saw'. Folding it in would make the one consequential number the least visible.
inbox-unread-max-age ships UNSET, asserted by a test, because a default would discard unread notifications on the upgrade that introduced it.

preferences.fallback is Map<String,String> keyed by category-class NAME, not Map<CategoryClass,ChannelType>: the settings package is deliberately free of service-layer types because every layer reads it and so it must depend on nothing (README deviation 5, and NotificationRuntimeProperties#channels is keyed by name for the same reason). Resolved to enums at the one consuming boundary, where an unknown name throws rather than silently meaning 'no fallback'.

the fallback uses a loop-scoped list of this recipient's deliveries rather than filtering the request-wide list: NotificationDeliveryEntity has no single recipient-reference column (a recipient is a user id OR an address), so a filter would have had to reconstruct the identity it was grouping by - a second place for two notions of 'same recipient' to disagree.

DESIGN BOUNDARY found while testing and deliberately NOT widened: the fallback fires only when every interrupting delivery is SUPPRESSED. A DEAD delivery (no destination at all - e.g. a user with no chat handle) does not trigger it. That is defensible - a refusal is a preference the inbox respects, while an unreachable address is an operational problem falling back would hide - but it is arguably the more useful trigger and the specs say SUPPRESSED, so it stays as specified and is recorded as an open question rather than answered unilaterally. Pinned by SuppressionFallbackIT#fallbackDoesNotFireOnUnreachableChannels.

SuppressionFallbackIT is the one test class that enables the chat channel (it ships disabled): it is the only test needing TWO interrupting channels, since 'every channel suppressed' and 'one channel survived' differ only when there is more than one. Without it the missing-bean guard skipped chat and both cases collapsed into the single-channel one - the first version of the class passed its own assertions while proving half of what it claimed.

RecipientFixtures gained givenUserWithChat: without a chat handle an opted-out chat delivery settles DEAD rather than SUPPRESSED, which silently breaks any assertion that was really about preferences.

9.2: the two READMEs now match section for section through 'Deviations and known gaps', and the new inbox section matches 6 subsections to 6. The one EN-only top-level section is 'Build and test', which README.ru.md never had - pre-existing drift, not introduced here and not in scope to add.

9.3: notification-service had NO OpenAPI test. Wrote InboxOpenApiIT covering the published paths, that no inbox operation declares an owner parameter under any spelling, and that the indistinguishable-404 and idempotence contracts appear in the published descriptions. Deliberately NOT a whole-document snapshot: one would fail on every unrelated endpoint change, and the usual response to that is to regenerate without reading the diff, which is worse than no test.
README test count updated from 208 to the real 340 (242 surefire + 98 failsafe), taken from the build output rather than estimated.

gate run in full at the end: manifest stale clean, image pins clean, migrations clean (16 changelogs / 86 changesets), mvn -q validate clean across every module, mvn -pl :notification-service -am verify BUILD SUCCESS with 242 unit + 102 integration and all coverage checks met, 0 in-repo dependents, openspec validate --strict valid. check_api_baseline remains failing for the environmental reason recorded in failures.
failures: scripts/check_api_baseline.sh cannot pass in this environment, and not because of this change: it reports an unresolvable published baseline for 25 modules (odata-filter, audit-core, db-core, job-core, security, web-core, jira-client, checkstyle-rules and 17 more), none of which this change touches, and notification-service - the only module it does touch - is a service and has no published baseline at all. The script is correct to fail rather than let revapi compare against an empty archive and report a false pass. It needs access to the releases repository or a populated local repository. Not retried: no number of attempts fixes a missing artifact repository.
open_questions: does the unread count need a bounded '99+' form on a very large inbox? deferrable - no schema or spec impact
should a dismissed item be purgeable sooner than inbox-ttl? deferrable - one property's default, the anchor already covers dismissed_at
phases 5-9 are not started: the recipient-facing read API, retention, the suppression fallback and the bilingual README. The write side (phases 1-4) is complete and verified.

should the fallback also fire when every requested channel settled DEAD (unreachable) rather than SUPPRESSED (refused)? Arguably the more valuable trigger - it is the 'user has no verified address' case from the proposal's Why - but it is a product decision and the specs say SUPPRESSED. Currently pinned by a test either way.
